tool.name: Dart
tool.tagline: Client-optimized language with sound null safety, behind Flutter
tool.description: Dart is Google's statically typed, garbage-collected language with sound null safety, async/await, records and pattern matching. It compiles ahead of time to native code for mobile and desktop, to JavaScript or WebAssembly for the web, and runs with a JIT and hot reload during development. Learn it to build Flutter apps and command-line or server tools in one approachable language.

glossary.def: A marker starting with @ attached to code for the compiler or tools, such as `@override`.
To take a value apart into named pieces with a pattern, as in `final (a, b) = pair;`.
The programming language that web browsers run. Dart code for websites is translated into JavaScript (or WebAssembly).
The type of a function value in Dart, written like `int Function(int, int)`: what it takes and what it returns.
A named value that can never change. In Dart a `const` value is fixed when the program is compiled, and identical constants are shared.
In Dart, a description of a value's shape, like `> 5`, `(a, b)` or `{'name': String name}`, that is checked against a value and can give names to its parts.
Covering every possible case. A Dart switch expression must be exhaustive, or the program doesn't compile.
Dart's `switch (value) { pattern => result, ... }`: it produces the result of the first case whose pattern fits, and must cover every possible value.
Dart's `=> expression` shorthand for a function body that just returns one expression: `int double(int x) => x * 2;`.
A type that can never hold null, like Dart's `String` or `int`. Add `?` (as in `String?`) to make it nullable.
Dart operators that handle null safely: `??` (use a fallback), `??=` (assign if null) and `?.` (only continue if not null).
Dart treating a variable as a more specific type after a check, such as a `String?` as a `String` after `if (s != null)`.
A Dart variable marked `late`: it gets its value later, or computes it the first time it is read. Reading it before it has a value is an error.
Dart's guarantee that values of non-nullable types are never null, checked at compile time.
Dart's `...` inside a collection literal, which copies in every item of another collection: `[...a, ...b]`.
An `if` written inside a Dart collection literal that adds an item only when its condition holds: `['home', if (loggedIn) 'profile']`.
A `for` written inside a Dart collection literal that adds an item for each round of the loop: `[for (final n in nums) n * n]`.
The part of a Dart constructor after `:` that sets fields before the constructor's body runs.
An extra Dart constructor with its own name, like `Point.origin()`, offering another way to create an object.
A Dart constructor marked `const` for classes whose fields are all final; calling it with `const` builds the object at compile time.
A Dart constructor marked `factory` that may return an existing object or a ready-made one instead of always creating a new one.
A member that looks like a field but runs code to produce its value each time it is read. A setter is the matching member for assigning.
To stop and signal an error by sending an exception up to the calling code, which may catch it.
In Dart, every class also acts as an interface: the list of its public members, which other classes can promise to provide with `implements`.
Dart's `super.name` constructor parameter, which passes the argument straight on to the parent class's constructor.
How Dart orders mixins: they are applied left to right, each on top of the previous one, so later ones win when two define the same method.
A Dart enum that, like a class, has fields, a const constructor, methods or interfaces.
A placeholder for a type in a generic class or function, like `T` in `Box<T>`, filled in when the class or function is used.
Generics whose type arguments still exist while the program runs, so Dart can check `x is List<int>`.
Dart's type for a value (or an error) that will be ready later, such as the reply to a network request.
Dart's keyword for pausing an async function until a Future finishes, then continuing with its value, without blocking the rest of the program.
A Dart value that bundles a fixed number of other values, like `(1, 'a')` or `(name: 'Ana', age: 31)`. Records are equal when their fields are equal.
Dart's package manager: `dart pub` adds, downloads and updates packages listed in pubspec.yaml, mostly from pub.dev.
The `pubspec.yaml` file that names a Dart package, says which Dart versions it supports and lists its dependencies.
Dart's code checker: it finds errors, warnings and style problems without running the code. Run it with `dart analyze`.
The connection created when you listen to a Dart stream; you can pause, resume and cancel it.
A Dart stream that many listeners can listen to at once; values sent when nobody listens are lost.
Dart's default kind of stream: exactly one listener, and values wait until it starts listening.
A Dart object you push values into with `add`; its `stream` delivers them to listeners.
A Dart class marked `sealed` whose direct subclasses must all be in the same library, so a switch over it can be checked for completeness.
A Dart keyword such as `base`, `interface`, `final` or `sealed` before `class` that limits how other libraries may extend or implement it.
A Dart declaration that adds methods or getters to an existing type you don't control, such as String.
A Dart compile-time wrapper around an existing type, like an int used as a user ID: it has its own name and methods, but is just the int at runtime.
In Dart tests, a value passed to `expect` that describes what to check, like `equals(3)`, `isNull` or `throwsA(...)`.
A small task in Dart's microtask queue. All waiting microtasks run before the event loop takes the next event, such as a timer.
The queue of outside events, such as timers, input and finished file reads, that Dart's event loop handles one at a time.
An independent Dart worker with its own memory and event loop. Isolates share no data and talk only by sending messages, which lets Dart use several processor cores.
Ahead-of-time compilation: turning the whole program into machine code before it runs, for fast startup. Dart uses it for release builds.
Removing code the program never uses when building it, so the finished app is smaller.
Writing a tool that produces source code for you, such as JSON conversion methods, as part of the build.

concepts.name: Programs, Dart and your first program
concepts.summary: What a program is, how Dart turns the text you write into something your computer runs, and how to run your first program.
concepts.why: Every later lesson writes and runs Dart code, so it helps to know what happens between typing text and seeing a result.
concepts.body:
A **program** is a list of instructions for a computer, the way a recipe is a list of steps for a cook. The computer follows them exactly, one after another, and never guesses what you meant.

Programmers write those instructions as text in a **programming language**. Dart is one, made by Google and used to build Flutter apps for phones, websites and desktops, as well as small tools. The text you write is called **source code**; Dart files end in `.dart`.

The chip that actually carries out instructions, the processor (or **CPU**), can't read Dart. It only understands **machine code**: long lists of numbers. A **compiler** is a program that translates source code into machine code; that translation is called **compiling**. For websites, Dart is translated into JavaScript, the language web browsers run, instead.

Before anything runs, Dart checks your code. Mistakes it can spot, such as a typo or using a number where text is expected, are reported as a **compile error** that points at the exact line. The moment of checking and translating is called **compile time**; the moment the program actually runs is called **runtime**. Every mistake caught at compile time is one your users never see.

To get started, install the Dart **SDK** (software development kit: the compiler plus its helper tools) from dart.dev; it also comes with Flutter. You use it by typing commands in a **terminal**: a text window where you type a command, press Enter and read the reply.

`dart create hello` creates a folder with a ready-made project. Inside it, `dart run` compiles and runs the program in one step. When the program is finished, `dart compile exe` builds an **executable**: a file that runs on its own, like any app on your computer.

Every Dart program starts at `void main() { ... }`. The lines between the curly braces run from top to bottom. `print('Hello, world!');` shows a line of text in the terminal. A piece of text between quotation marks is called a **string**. Each instruction is a **statement**, and statements end with a semicolon.

Two more commands you will use constantly: `dart analyze` checks your code for mistakes without running it, and `dart format` tidies its layout.
takeaways: Source code is the text you write; the compiler translates it into something the computer runs
Dart checks your code at compile time and reports mistakes before the program runs
Every program starts at `main`; `print` shows a line of text; statements end with `;`
pitfalls: Skimming past an error message: it names the line and usually says exactly what is wrong.

quiz.q: What does a compiler do?
options: Translates source code into a form the computer can run, checking it for mistakes
quiz.explain: A compiler turns the text you write into machine code (or JavaScript for the web), and Dart's compiler reports mistakes it finds on the way.

quiz.q: Which command compiles and runs a Dart project in one step?
quiz.explain: `dart run` compiles the project and runs it; `dart create` makes a new project, `dart analyze` only checks it, and `dart format` tidies it.

concepts.name: Variables, types, final and const
concepts.summary: Store values in variables with var, final and const, and meet Dart's basic types: whole numbers, decimals, text and true/false.
concepts.why: Every Dart program and Flutter app stores values in variables, and the difference between final and const matters for speed in Flutter.
concepts.body:
Programs keep track of values: a score, a name, a price. A **variable** is a name for a value, like a label on a box. `var name = 'Dart';` creates a variable called `name` holding the text `Dart`. Later you can give it a new value: `name = 'Flutter';`.

Every value has a **data type**: the kind of value it is, which decides what you can do with it. Numbers come in two types: `int` for an **integer** (a whole number such as -3 or 42), and `double` for a **floating-point number** (a number with a decimal point, such as 3.75).

Text has the type `String`. The type `bool` is a **boolean**: a value that is either `true` or `false`.

With `var`, Dart works out the type from the value you give it, which is called **type inference**. You can also write the type yourself instead of `var`, a **type annotation**: `int count = 0;`. Either way the type is then fixed: a variable that holds a `String` can only ever hold strings.

A `final` variable can be set only once: `final now = DateTime.now();`. Its value is worked out while the program runs, and afterwards it never changes.

A `const` variable holds a **constant**, a value already fixed at compile time: `const maxItems = 100;`. Dart keeps one shared copy of each identical constant, and Flutter uses this to skip redrawing parts of the screen that are `const`.

Strings use single or double quotation marks. Put a variable's value into a string with `$name`, or the result of a calculation with `${...}`: `'Total: ${price * 2}'`. This is called **string interpolation**. Three quotation marks together start text that can span several lines.

Dart never mixes text and numbers on its own, so you do the **type conversion** yourself: `int.parse('42')` turns text into a number, `3.7.toInt()` drops the decimals, and `n.toString()` turns a number into text. Division with `/` always gives a `double` (`7 / 2` is 3.5); `~/` divides and drops the remainder (`7 ~/ 2` is 3).

Dart is **statically typed**: it checks types at compile time, and the check is sound, so a variable of type `int` really holds an `int` when the program runs. The special type `dynamic` turns these checks off for a variable; avoid it, because mistakes then only show up at runtime.
concepts.code:
void main() {
  var language = 'Dart';           // type inferred: String
  int year = 2011;                 // type written out
  final launched = DateTime(year); // a date; can be set only once
  const maxScore = 100;            // fixed at compile time

  year += 14;                      // add 14 to year
  print('$language turns ${year - launched.year}');  // Dart turns 14

  double ratio = 7 / 2;            // / always gives a double
  int whole = 7 ~/ 2;              // divide and drop the remainder
  print('$ratio $whole');          // 3.5 3

  print(int.parse('42') + maxScore);  // 142
  const a = [1, 2];                // a constant list of numbers
  const b = [1, 2];
  print(identical(a, b));          // true: identical constants are one value
}
takeaways: `var` infers the type, `final` is set once, `const` is fixed at compile time
`int` and `double` hold numbers, `String` text, `bool` true or false
`/` always gives a double; `~/` divides whole numbers; insert values into text with `$x` and `${...}`
pitfalls: Using `dynamic` to make type errors go away, which only moves them to runtime, where users meet them.

quiz.q: What is the difference between `final` and `const`?
options: const must be known at compile time; final is set once while the program runs
quiz.explain: A final value can't change after it is first set, while a const value must already be fixed when the code is compiled.

quiz.q: What is the value of `7 ~/ 2`?
quiz.explain: `~/` divides and drops the remainder, so 7 ~/ 2 is 3; `7 / 2` would be 3.5.

concepts.name: Operators and control flow
concepts.summary: Make decisions with if, else and switch, and repeat work with for and while loops.
concepts.why: Choosing between actions and repeating them are things every program does, and Dart 3's switch expressions replace many long if/else chains.
concepts.body:
Programs often have to choose: if the password is right, let the user in; otherwise, show an error. Code like that is a **conditional**: `if (age >= 18) { ... } else { ... }`. The first block runs only when the condition is true; `else if` adds more choices.

Signs such as `+`, `>=`, `==` (equal) and `!=` (not equal) are called **operators**. A condition must be a `bool`: Dart doesn't treat 0 or empty text as false. The operator `condition ? a : b` picks one of two values: `age >= 18 ? 'adult' : 'child'`.

To repeat work you write a **loop**; each trip through it is one **iteration**:

- `for (var i = 0; i < n; i++)` counts: start `i` at 0, keep going while `i < n`, and add 1 to `i` (`i++`) after each round.
- `for (final item in items)` goes through each item of a collection, such as a list (lists come in a later lesson).
- `while (condition) { }` repeats as long as the condition stays true; `do { } while (condition);` always runs at least once.
- `break` leaves a loop early and `continue` skips to the next round.

`switch` compares a value against a list of **patterns**, descriptions of what a value may look like, and runs the code of the first one that fits. Unlike in some older languages, a case with code never runs on into the next case, so no `break` is needed.

A **switch expression** produces a value:

```dart
final label = switch (code) {
  200 => 'ok',
  404 => 'not found',
  >= 500 => 'server error',
  _ => 'other',
};
```

Each case is `pattern => value`, separated by commas. Patterns can be values (`200`), comparisons (`>= 500`) or combinations with `||` (or) and `&&` (and), and `_` matches anything. A switch expression must be **exhaustive**: it has to cover every possible value, and the compiler checks that it does. That is what the `_` case is for here.

Other useful operators: `%` gives the remainder of a division, `is` checks a value's type, and `as` tells Dart to treat a value as a given type.
takeaways: Conditions must be real `true`/`false` values
`for`, `for`-`in` and `while` repeat work; `break` and `continue` steer a loop
Switch expressions `pattern => value` must cover every possible value
pitfalls: Writing `case 1:` and `case 2:` each with code and expecting the first to run on into the second, as in older languages.

quiz.q: What does `switch (7) { > 5 => 'big', _ => 'small' }` produce?
quiz.explain: The pattern `> 5` fits 7, so the first case's value, 'big', is produced.

quiz.q: How many times does the body of `for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) { }` run?
quiz.explain: i takes the values 0, 1 and 2; when it reaches 3 the condition i < 3 is false and the loop ends.

concepts.name: Functions and parameters
concepts.summary: Write your own functions with inputs and a result, using positional, optional and named parameters, arrow syntax and closures.
concepts.why: Functions let you name a piece of work and reuse it, and Flutter uses named parameters and functions passed as values everywhere.
concepts.body:
A **function** is a named, reusable piece of code, like a recipe you write once and follow whenever you need it. You already know `main` and `print`. Running a function is called calling it: write its name followed by parentheses.

Here is one: `int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }`. First comes the type of the result (`int`), then the name, then the **parameters**: named inputs, each with a type. The values you pass in when calling, as in `add(2, 3)`, are the **arguments**. `return` hands back the result, the **return value**. A function that returns nothing has the type `void`.

An **expression** is a piece of code that produces a value, like `a + b`. When a function's body is a single expression, you can use **arrow syntax**: `int add(int a, int b) => a + b;`.

Parameters come in three kinds:

- **Required positional**: `f(int a)`; callers must pass them, in order.
- **Optional positional**, in square brackets: `f(int a, [int b = 0])`; here `b` is 0 when left out.
- **Named**, in curly braces: `f({required String name, int age = 0})`. Callers write the name: `f(name: 'Ana')`. Named parameters are optional unless marked `required`, and an optional one needs a default value (or a type that allows "no value", explained in the next lesson).

A function can't have both optional positional and named parameters. Flutter uses named parameters almost everywhere because calls read clearly: `Padding(padding: ..., child: ...)`.

In Dart a function is a value, like a number: you can store it in a variable, pass it to another function and return it from one. Its type is written like `int Function(int, int)`. A function without a name, written right where it is used, such as `(x) => x * 2`, is called an anonymous function or **lambda**.

A function that uses variables from the code around it is a **closure**. It keeps those variables alive, even after the surrounding function has finished, and sees any later changes to them.

`typedef Compare = int Function(String a, String b);` gives a function type a short name. You can also pass an existing function by name, without calling it: `names.forEach(print)` calls `print` on each name.
takeaways: Named parameters `{...}` are optional unless marked `required`
`=>` is shorthand for a body that is a single expression
Functions are values you can pass around; closures keep the variables they use
pitfalls: Forgetting `required` on a named parameter that can't be null and has no default value, which is a compile error.

quiz.q: Given `void f(int a, {int b = 1})`, which call is valid?
quiz.explain: `a` is required and passed by position, while `b` is named, so it must be written `b: 2`.

concepts.name: Sound null safety
concepts.summary: Mark values that may be missing with ?, handle them safely with ??, ?. and null checks, and use late for values set later.
concepts.why: Null safety removes one of the most common kinds of crash, and all of Dart's and Flutter's own code is written with it.
concepts.body:
Sometimes a variable has no value yet, such as the nickname of a user who never chose one. Dart represents "no value" with **null**. In many languages, using a null by mistake as if it were a real value is one of the most common causes of crashes.

In Dart, types are **non-nullable** by default: a `String` variable can never hold null. Add `?` to allow it: `String? nickname;` has a **nullable** type, and it starts out as null. Variables of non-nullable types must be given a value before they are used.

Dart has **operators** (symbols like `+` that work on values) made for nullable values:

- `a ?? b` gives `a`, or `b` if `a` is null.
- `x ??= value` assigns only if `x` is null.
- `text?.length` gives null if `text` is null, otherwise its length.
- `value!` means "I'm sure this isn't null"; if it is, the program stops with an error. Use it sparingly.

Dart follows your checks. After `if (name != null)`, it knows `name` can't be null inside that block and treats it as a plain `String`. This is called **type promotion**, and it also happens after an early `return`. It works for **local variables** (variables created inside a function), but not for values stored inside objects, which could change between the check and the use (the classes lesson explains why).

`late` marks a non-nullable variable that will get its value later: `late final String token;`. Reading it before it is set is an error at runtime. With a starting value, as in `late final total = compute();`, the calculation runs only the first time the variable is read.

Since Dart 3.8, a list can contain `?item`, which adds the item only if it isn't null: `[1, ?maybe]` (lists come in a later lesson).

The guarantee is sound: once your program and all the code it uses are null-safe, a value of a non-nullable type can never be null at runtime.
takeaways: Types can't hold null unless marked with `?`
Prefer `??`, `?.` and null checks over `!`
After a null check, Dart treats a local variable as non-null
pitfalls: Expecting a value stored in an object to be treated as non-null after `if (obj.field != null)`; copy it into a local variable first.

quiz.q: What does `String? name; print(name ?? 'nobody');` print?
quiz.explain: `name` is null, so `??` uses the value on its right.

quiz.q: Why can't you write `String s = null;` in Dart?
quiz.explain: Types are non-nullable by default; only `String?` may hold null.

concepts.name: Lists, sets and maps
concepts.summary: Keep many values together in lists, sets and maps, and build them with collection if, collection for and the spread operator.
concepts.why: Collections hold almost all app data, and collection if and for are how Flutter builds lists of things to show on screen.
concepts.body:
Programs usually handle many values at once: a shopping list, a set of tags, phone numbers stored by name. Dart has three main collections:

- A `List` keeps items in order: `var nums = [1, 2, 3];`. Each item has a position number, its **index**, counting from 0, so `nums[0]` is the first item.
- A `Set` holds each item at most once: `var tags = {'dart', 'flutter'};`.
- A `Map` stores **key-value pairs**, so you can look a value up by its key: `var ages = {'ana': 31, 'bo': 25};` and then `ages['ana']` is 31.

The type in angle brackets says what a collection holds: `List<int>` is a list of whole numbers, `Map<String, int>` maps text to numbers. Values written directly in code, like `[1, 2, 3]` or `'hi'`, are called **literals**. An empty `{}` is a Map; write `<String>{}` for an empty Set and `<int>[]` for an empty list.

Collections come with **methods**, functions you call with a dot after a value: `nums.add(4)`, `addAll`, `insert`, `removeAt`, `contains`, `indexOf`, `sort`, plus `nums.length`, `first` and `last`. Asking for a position that doesn't exist, like `nums[10]` in a three-item list, stops the program with a `RangeError`.

Looking up a missing key, such as `ages['zoe']`, gives null, so the result's type is nullable (`int?`). Use `containsKey`, `putIfAbsent` or `update` to handle missing keys. `for (final entry in ages.entries)` goes through every pair as `entry.key` and `entry.value`.

Collection literals have special forms:

- **Spread** `...` copies all items of another collection in: `[...a, ...b]`; `...?maybeList` skips it if it is null.
- **Collection if** adds an item only when a condition holds: `['home', if (loggedIn) 'profile']`.
- **Collection for** adds an item per round of a loop: `[for (final n in nums) n * n]`.

This is how Flutter describes what is on screen: `children: [Header(), if (showBanner) Banner(), for (final m in messages) Tile(m)]`.

Collections can be changed (they are **mutable**) unless created with `const` or `List.unmodifiable`, which makes them **immutable**. A `final` variable holding a list can't be pointed at another list, but the items inside can still change.
takeaways: `[...]` is a List, `{a, b}` a Set, `{k: v}` a Map; `{}` alone is a Map
Collection if, collection for and spread `...` build collections in place
Looking up a map key gives a nullable value
pitfalls: Writing `var s = {};` expecting a Set, and getting an empty Map.

quiz.q: What does `[1, if (false) 2, for (var i in [3, 4]) i * 2]` produce?
quiz.explain: The if adds nothing when its condition is false, and the for adds 3 * 2 and 4 * 2.

concepts.name: Classes and constructors
concepts.summary: Define your own types with classes: fields, methods, getters, and the different kinds of constructors.
concepts.why: Everything in Flutter is a class, and Flutter's building blocks rely on const and named constructors.
concepts.body:
A **class** is a blueprint for your own type of value. `class Point { ... }` describes what every point holds and can do. Each value built from the blueprint is an **object**, also called an **instance** of the class: `Point(3, 4)` creates one.

A class keeps data in **fields**, variables that belong to each object, like `x` and `y`. Read one with a dot: `p.x`. Its behaviour lives in **methods**, functions that belong to the class, also called with a dot: `p.distanceTo(q)`.

A **constructor** is the special function that creates an object and fills in its fields; it has the class's name. Every field that can't be null must get a value before the constructor's body runs. The common forms:

- `Point(this.x, this.y);` copies the arguments straight into the fields. Named version: `Person({required this.name, this.age = 0});`.
- An **initializer list** after `:` sets fields before the body runs: `Rect(double w) : width = w, height = w * 2;`.
- A **named constructor** offers another way to build one: `Point.origin() : x = 0, y = 0;`.
- A **const constructor**, for classes whose fields are all `final`: `const Point(1, 2)` is then built at compile time, and identical constants are shared.
- A **factory constructor** may hand back an object that already exists, or build one from data, such as text downloaded from the internet.

A **getter** looks like a field but computes its value each time: `double get area => width * height;`. Every field automatically comes with a getter (and a setter for assigning, unless it is `final`), so you can later turn a field into a getter without changing the code that uses it.

Names starting with an underscore, like `_cache`, are private: usable only in the same file. Dart calls each file a **library**, so privacy is per file, not per class.

By default `==` checks whether two variables refer to the very same object. For classes that represent a value, like a point, **override** (replace with your own version, marked `@override`) `==`, `hashCode` (a number that sets and maps use to find objects quickly) and `toString`. No `new` is needed: just call `Point(1, 2)`.
takeaways: `this.x` parameters and initializer lists fill in final fields
Named, const and factory constructors cover most ways of creating objects
`_name` is private to the file (library), not to the class
pitfalls: Overriding `==` without also overriding `hashCode`, which makes sets and maps lose track of your objects.

quiz.q: Where is a member named `_cache` visible?
options: Only in classes built on top of it
quiz.explain: Dart privacy is per library: names starting with an underscore are visible throughout the file that declares them.

concepts.name: Iterables and collection methods
concepts.summary: Transform data with map, where, fold, expand and any, and understand that map and where are lazy.
concepts.why: Most data shaping in Dart and Flutter is a chain of these methods, and knowing when they actually run explains some surprising behaviour.
concepts.body:
An **iterable** is anything you can go through item by item. Lists and sets are iterables, and so are a map's `keys`, `values` and `entries`. In Dart they all share the type `Iterable`, which offers many methods that take a function and apply it to the items:

- `map(f)`: transform each item.
- `where(test)`: keep the items that pass a test; `whereType<T>()` keeps items of one type.
- `expand(f)`: turn each item into several and flatten them into one sequence.
- `fold(start, combine)` and `reduce(combine)`: combine all items into one value, such as a total.
- `any`, `every`, `contains`, `firstWhere(test, orElse: ...)`.
- `take`, `skip`, `takeWhile`, `skipWhile`.
- `join(', ')`, `toList()`, `toSet()`.

Key fact: `map`, `where`, `expand` and similar methods are **lazy**. They don't do the work right away; they return an `Iterable` that runs your function each time someone goes through it. Go through it twice and the function runs twice; never go through it and the function never runs.

Call `.toList()` when you need a finished list you can reuse, or when something requires a real `List`, as Flutter often does.

A separate add-on package, `collection`, adds helpers such as `groupBy`, `sortedBy` and deep equality checks. Dart 3 itself has `firstOrNull`, `lastOrNull` and `indexed`, which gives each item together with its position.

`sort` changes the list itself and returns nothing (`void`), so you can't chain another method after it; make a copy first if you need the original order.
takeaways: `map` and `where` are lazy; call `toList()` to get a finished list
`fold` combines items starting from a value you give; `reduce` needs at least one item
`sort` changes the list itself and returns nothing
pitfalls: Passing `items.map(...)` where a `List` is required, or going through an expensive lazy chain many times.

quiz.q: `final it = [1, 2, 3].map(f);` How many times has `f` run after this line alone?
quiz.explain: map is lazy: f only runs when something goes through the resulting Iterable.

concepts.name: Exceptions and error handling
concepts.summary: Signal and handle errors with throw, try, on, catch and finally, and know when to use Exception or Error.
concepts.why: Reading files, turning text into numbers and talking to other computers can all fail, and catching the right kind of failure keeps apps from crashing or hiding mistakes.
takeaways: Throw `Exception`s for problems the caller can recover from; `Error`s mean bugs
`on Type catch (e, s)` catches one kind; `rethrow` passes it on; `finally` always runs
Prefer non-throwing versions like `tryParse` for input that may well be wrong
pitfalls: A bare `catch (e)` that swallows everything, including real bugs.

quiz.q: Which clause catches only FormatException and gives you access to it?
quiz.explain: Dart uses `on Type` to choose the kind and `catch (e)` to name the exception.

concepts.name: Inheritance, abstract classes and interfaces
concepts.summary: Extend classes, override members, write abstract classes, and implement any class as an interface.
concepts.why: Flutter's widget hierarchy and most APIs depend on extends and implements, and Dart treats them differently from Java.
concepts.body:
**Inheritance** lets one class build on another: `class Dog extends Animal` makes `Dog` a **subclass** that gets all of `Animal`'s fields and methods, and `Animal` is its superclass. Override members with the `@override` annotation (a marker for the compiler) and call the parent's version with `super.method()`. Constructors aren't inherited; a subclass constructor forwards with `super(...)`, or more concisely with **super parameters**: `Dog(super.name);`.

An **abstract class** can't be used to create objects directly and can declare methods without bodies, which concrete subclasses must implement:

```dart
abstract class Shape {
  double get area;           // abstract getter
  String describe() => 'Shape with area $area';
}
```

An **interface** is a list of members a type promises to provide. Dart has no separate interface declaration in the Java sense: **every class implicitly defines an interface** made of its public members. `class MockClient implements HttpClient` must provide all of them itself — nothing is inherited. A class can `extends` only one class but `implements` many.

Use `extends` to reuse code and `implements` to promise a set of members (common for fake versions of classes used in tests). Since Dart 3, class modifiers such as `interface`, `base` and `final` let library authors restrict which of these is allowed outside their library.

`Object` is the root of all non-nullable types. `toString`, `==`, `hashCode` and `noSuchMethod` come from it.

Type tests with `is` promote: `if (shape is Circle) print(shape.radius);`. To narrow a parameter's type in an overriding method, mark the parameter `covariant`.
takeaways: `extends` inherits code from one superclass
Every class is an implicit interface; `implements` copies only the contract
Abstract classes declare members subclasses must provide
pitfalls: Using `implements` and expecting to inherit method bodies.

quiz.q: `class B implements A` where A has a concrete method `hello()`. What must B do?
quiz.explain: implements takes only A's interface, so B must implement every member itself.

concepts.name: Mixins
concepts.summary: Reuse behavior across unrelated classes with mixin declarations and the with clause.
concepts.why: A class can extend only one parent, but often needs several small, unrelated abilities, such as logging or saving; mixins let it reuse code from more than one source.
takeaways: `with A, B` layers mixins left to right; later ones override earlier ones
`mixin M on Base` restricts use and allows `super` calls
Mixins have no constructors; declare with `mixin` or `mixin class`
pitfalls: Relying on mixin order without realizing a later mixin silently overrides an earlier method.

quiz.q: `class C extends Base with A, B` and both A and B override `run()`, calling super. Which runs first when calling `C().run()`?
options: B's run(), which calls A's via super
quiz.explain: Mixins are linearized left to right, so B is the outermost layer and its super is A.

concepts.name: Enhanced enums
concepts.summary: Declare enums with fields, constructors, methods and interfaces, and switch over them exhaustively.
concepts.why: Enums model fixed sets like states and themes, and exhaustive switches catch missed cases at compile time.
takeaways: Enums can have final fields, a const constructor, methods and interfaces
Switches over enums are exhaustive without `default`
Use `name` and `values.byName` to save and load enum values
pitfalls: Adding `_ =>` to every enum switch, which hides newly added values.

quiz.q: What must an enhanced enum's constructor be?
quiz.explain: Enum values are compile-time constants, so the generative constructor must be const.

concepts.name: Generics
concepts.summary: Write generic classes and functions, limit type parameters with extends, and understand that Dart keeps type arguments at runtime.
concepts.why: Typed collections, Futures and Flutter widgets like ValueListenableBuilder<T> are generic, and you'll write your own.
takeaways: Type parameters keep code reusable and type-safe
`T extends Bound` lets you call the bound's members
Generics are reified: `is List<int>` is checked at run time
pitfalls: Relying on covariance and adding a wider type to a narrower list, which throws at run time.

quiz.q: What is printed by `Object x = <int>[]; print(x is List<String>);`?
quiz.explain: Dart keeps type arguments at run time, so a List<int> is not a List<String>.

concepts.name: Futures and async/await
concepts.summary: Work with Future, async and await, handle errors, and run independent futures at the same time with Future.wait.
concepts.why: Every network call, file read and database query in Dart and Flutter returns a Future.
concepts.body:
Some work takes a while: downloading data, reading a file, querying a database. **Asynchronous** code starts such work and carries on instead of waiting. A **`Future<T>`** represents a value (or error) that will be available later.

Dart runs your code on a single **thread**, one line of work (each isolate, a later lesson, has its own). So functions that read files or talk to the network return futures instead of **blocking**, which would make the whole program sit and wait.

Mark a function `async` and use **`await`** to wait for a future without blocking:

```dart
Future<User> loadUser(int id) async {
  final json = await api.get('/users/$id');
  return User.fromJson(json);
}
```

An `async` function always returns a `Future`, even if the body returns a plain value. Use `Future<void>` when nothing is returned. Errors from awaited futures are thrown at the `await`, so ordinary `try`/`catch`/`finally` works.

Important behaviors:

- An `async` function runs synchronously until its first `await`, then returns the future to its caller.
- Sequential `await`s run one after another. For independent work, start the futures first and wait together: `await Future.wait([a(), b()])`, or with records `final (u, p) = await (loadUser(), loadPosts()).wait;`.
- `.timeout(Duration(...))` fails a slow future with a `TimeoutException`.
- A future you forget to await runs anyway, but its errors are never caught. Turn on the `unawaited_futures` lint (a rule for the analyzer) and wrap calls you deliberately don't wait for in `unawaited(...)`.

`Future.delayed`, `Future.value` and `Completer` create futures yourself; `Completer` turns code that reports its result through a **callback** (a function you hand over to be called later) into a future.
takeaways: `async` functions return a Future; `await` unwraps it
Start independent futures together and wait with `Future.wait` or `(a, b).wait`
Errors surface at `await` and are caught with try/catch
pitfalls: Forgetting `await`, so errors go uncaught and code runs out of order.

quiz.q: `final x = loadUser();` inside an async function, without await. What is x?
quiz.explain: Without await you get the Future itself, not its eventual value.

concepts.name: Records and patterns
concepts.summary: Return multiple values with records, and destructure and match data with patterns in variables, switch and if-case.
concepts.why: Records and patterns are Dart 3's biggest additions and make JSON handling and state matching concise and safe.
concepts.body:
A **record** bundles a fixed number of values into one value that can't be changed: `(1, 'a')` or with named fields `(name: 'Ana', age: 31)`. Its type is written the same way: `(int, String)` or `({String name, int age})`. Positional fields are read with `$1`, `$2`; named ones by name. Two records are equal when their fields are equal, so they're great for returning several values from a function:

```dart
(double, double) minMax(List<double> xs) => (xs.reduce(min), xs.reduce(max));
final (lo, hi) = minMax(data);
```

**Patterns** describe the shape of a value and can **destructure** it, taking it apart into named pieces. They appear in:

- Variable declarations: `final (lo, hi) = ...;`, `var {'name': name} = json;`.
- `switch` statements and expressions.
- `if (value case pattern)` — match and bind in a condition.
- `for` loops: `for (final (i, x) in list.indexed)`.

Pattern kinds include constants, relational (`> 0`), logical (`||`, `&&`), records, lists (`[first, ...rest]`), maps (`{'id': int id}`), objects (`Point(x: 0, :var y)`), wildcards `_`, casts and null checks (`var x?`).

Map and list patterns check types as they bind, which makes validating untyped JSON clean: `if (json case {'name': String name, 'age': int age}) ...` only matches when both keys exist with the right types. A `when` clause adds an extra condition (a guard): `case (var a, var b) when a > b:`.
takeaways: Records `(a, b)` / `(name: x)` bundle values with structural equality
Patterns destructure in declarations, switch, if-case and for
Map/list patterns type-check while binding — ideal for JSON
pitfalls: Matching JSON numbers with `int` when the server may send `1.0`; use `num` and convert.

quiz.q: Does `{'id': int id}` match the map `{'id': 7, 'extra': true}`?
options: No, extra keys make map patterns fail
Yes, map patterns ignore keys they don't mention
quiz.explain: Map patterns only check the listed keys; unmentioned keys are allowed.

concepts.name: Libraries, packages and pub
concepts.summary: Split code into files (libraries), bring in other code with import, and add packages other people wrote with dart pub.
concepts.why: Real projects use packages from pub.dev and are split into files that each offer a clear set of public names.
concepts.body:
Every Dart file is a **library**. To **import** another library means making its public names usable in your file:

- `import 'dart:math';` — core libraries.
- `import 'package:http/http.dart' as http;` — a package, with a **prefix** to avoid name clashes.
- `import 'src/utils.dart';` — a relative path within your package.
- `show` and `hide` limit which names are imported: `import 'dart:math' show max, pi;`.

Privacy is per library: `_names` are private to the file. Big libraries can be split with `part`/`part of`, but most code just uses separate libraries. The part of a package other code may use (its **API**) lives in `lib/`, with implementation in `lib/src/` and a top-level file that `export`s what users should see.

A **package** is a folder of Dart code with a `pubspec.yaml` file, its **pubspec**, declaring its name, the Dart versions it supports (`environment: sdk: ^3.9.0`), its **dependencies** (packages it uses) and `dev_dependencies` (packages needed only while developing, such as test tools). Versions follow **semantic versioning**, where the first number changes only for updates that may break your code, and `http: ^1.2.0` means at least 1.2.0 but below 2.0.0.

Commands:

- `dart create my_app` — new project.
- `dart pub add http` / `dart pub add --dev test` — add dependencies.
- `dart pub get` — work out matching versions and download them; writes `pubspec.lock`, a **lock file** recording the exact versions (keep it with your code for apps).
- `dart pub outdated` and `dart pub upgrade`.
- `dart run`, `dart analyze`, `dart format`, `dart fix --apply`.

`analysis_options.yaml` configures the analyzer (`dart analyze`); `package:lints` provides a recommended set of rules.
concepts.code:
# pubspec.yaml
name: weather_cli
description: A tiny command-line weather client.
version: 1.0.0
environment:
  sdk: ^3.9.0

dependencies:
  http: ^1.2.0
  args: ^2.5.0

dev_dependencies:
  lints: ^5.0.0
  test: ^1.25.0

# lib/weather_cli.dart (the package's public API):
#   export 'src/client.dart' show WeatherClient;
# bin/main.dart:
#   import 'package:weather_cli/weather_cli.dart';
#   import 'package:http/http.dart' as http;
#   import 'dart:math' show max;
# Commands: dart pub get · dart run · dart analyze · dart test
takeaways: `import ... as p` and `show`/`hide` control names
Public API in `lib/`, internals in `lib/src/`, re-exported with `export`
`^1.2.0` allows compatible updates below 2.0.0
pitfalls: Importing another package's `src/` files directly — they're private implementation details.

quiz.q: What versions does the constraint `http: ^1.2.0` allow?
quiz.explain: Caret syntax allows any version compatible under semantic versioning, up to the next major.

concepts.name: Streams
concepts.summary: Consume and create streams with await for, listen, async* generators and StreamController, and know single vs broadcast.
concepts.why: Streams model things that happen again and again over time, such as user input, messages from a server, database changes and Flutter's StreamBuilder.
concepts.body:
A **`Stream<T>`** delivers a series of asynchronous events: data, errors, and a final "done". Where a `Future` gives one value, a stream gives many.

Consuming:

- `await for (final event in stream) { ... }` inside an `async` function, with `try`/`catch` for errors. The loop ends when the stream closes.
- `stream.listen(onData, onError: ..., onDone: ...)` returns a `StreamSubscription` you can `pause`, `resume` and must `cancel()` when done (for example in a Flutter `dispose`).

Streams have iterable-like transformers: `map`, `where`, `take`, `skip`, `distinct`, `asyncMap`, `expand`, plus `first`, `toList()` and `fold` that return futures.

Producing:

- An **`async*` generator**, a function that hands out values one by one with `yield` (and `yield*` to forward another stream). It's lazy: the body starts when someone listens and pauses when the listener pauses.
- A **`StreamController`** when events come from elsewhere: `controller.add(x)`, `addError`, `close()`, and expose `controller.stream`.

**Single-subscription** streams (the default, e.g. file reads) allow exactly one listener and hold on to events until it starts listening. **Broadcast** streams (`StreamController.broadcast()`, `asBroadcastStream()`) allow many listeners but drop events no one is listening to. Listening twice to a single-subscription stream throws a `StateError`.

For advanced operations, such as waiting until events stop arriving or combining several streams, the `rxdart` and `stream_transform` packages are common.
takeaways: Consume with `await for` or `listen`, and cancel subscriptions
Produce with `async*`/`yield` or a StreamController
Single-subscription = one listener; broadcast = many, no buffering
pitfalls: Never cancelling a `listen` subscription, leaking memory and work after a widget is gone.

quiz.q: What happens if you call listen twice on a default (single-subscription) StreamController's stream?
options: The first listener is replaced silently
The second listen throws a StateError
quiz.explain: Single-subscription streams allow exactly one listener; use broadcast for several.

concepts.name: Sealed classes and class modifiers
concepts.summary: Model closed type hierarchies with sealed classes for exhaustive switches, and control APIs with base, interface, final and mixin modifiers.
concepts.why: A sealed family of classes plus pattern matching lets you list every possible shape of a value, ideal for screen states, results and events.
concepts.body:
A **`sealed`** class is implicitly abstract and can only be extended or implemented **within its own library**. Because the compiler knows every direct subtype, a `switch` over a sealed type is checked for **exhaustiveness**:

```dart
sealed class Result<T> {}
class Ok<T> extends Result<T> { Ok(this.value); final T value; }
class Err<T> extends Result<T> { Err(this.error); final Object error; }
```

`switch (r) { Ok(:final value) => ..., Err(:final error) => ... }` needs no default, and adding a new subclass turns every incomplete switch into a compile error. This is the Dart 3 way to model UI states (`Loading`, `Loaded`, `Failed`), API results and events.

Dart 3 also adds modifiers that control how classes may be used **outside** their library:

- `base` — can be extended but not implemented; subclasses must be `base`, `final` or `sealed`. Guarantees your constructor and private members run.
- `interface` — can be implemented but not extended.
- `final` — neither extended nor implemented outside the library.
- `abstract` — can't be instantiated; combine with the others (`abstract interface class` is a pure interface).
- `mixin class` — usable as both a class and a mixin.

Inside the declaring library these restrictions don't apply. Use them when publishing packages to keep the freedom to evolve classes without breaking users.
takeaways: `sealed` = closed set of subtypes in one library, enabling exhaustive switches
Object patterns like `Loaded(:final items)` destructure fields
`base`, `interface`, `final` restrict extends/implements outside the library
pitfalls: Splitting a sealed hierarchy across files without `part`, which isn't allowed — subtypes must be in the same library.

quiz.q: Why can a switch over a sealed class omit a default case?
options: The compiler knows all direct subtypes and checks they are all handled
Defaults are never needed in Dart 3
quiz.explain: All direct subtypes must be in the same library, so the compiler can verify exhaustiveness.

concepts.name: Extension methods and extension types
concepts.summary: Add methods to existing types with extensions, and create zero-cost wrapper types with extension types.
concepts.why: Extensions keep helper code readable, and extension types give type safety for IDs, and for talking to JavaScript, at no runtime cost.
takeaways: Extensions add members, resolved by static type
Extension types are compile-time-only wrappers with zero run-time cost
Use extension types for typed IDs and interop, not for security
pitfalls: Calling an extension method on a `dynamic` value and getting a NoSuchMethodError.

quiz.q: At run time, what is a value of `extension type UserId(int value)`?
options: A UserId object wrapping an int
quiz.explain: Extension types are erased; at run time the representation value itself is used.

concepts.name: Testing and static analysis
concepts.summary: Write unit tests with package:test, use groups, setUp and matchers, test async code, and enforce lints with the analyzer.
concepts.why: Tests and lints are what keep a Dart codebase or Flutter app maintainable as it grows.
concepts.body:
`package:test` is the standard test framework (Flutter's `flutter_test` builds on it). Tests live in `test/` in files ending `_test.dart`, and run with `dart test`.

```dart
test('adds', () => expect(add(1, 2), 3));
```

Structure with `group('name', () { ... })`, and share setup code with `setUp` / `tearDown` (run around each test) and `setUpAll` / `tearDownAll` (once per group).

`expect(actual, matcher)` accepts values or **matchers**: `equals`, `isTrue`, `isNull`, `contains`, `hasLength`, `closeTo(3.14, 0.01)`, `isA<FormatException>()`, `throwsA(...)`, `throwsArgumentError`, `completion(...)` for futures and `emitsInOrder([...])` for streams.

Async tests just return a future: mark the body `async` and `await`. For code that throws, wrap the call: `expect(() => parse('x'), throwsFormatException)`.

Run a subset with `dart test --name 'parser'` or a single file. Use `package:mocktail` or `mockito` for fake versions of dependencies (mocks), though a hand-written class that `implements` the dependency is often simpler.

**Static analysis** catches problems without running the code: `dart analyze` reports errors, warnings and lints configured in `analysis_options.yaml`. Include `package:lints/recommended.yaml` (or `flutter_lints`) and add rules like `unawaited_futures` and `prefer_final_locals`. `dart format` gives one canonical style, and `dart fix --apply` auto-applies many suggestions. Run all three in CI, the automatic checks that run on every change.
takeaways: `test`, `group`, `setUp` and `expect` with matchers
Async tests are `async` functions; wrap throwing calls in a closure
Run `dart analyze`, `dart format` and tests in CI
pitfalls: Writing `expect(parse('x'), throwsA(...))` without the `() =>` closure, so the exception is thrown before expect sees it.

quiz.q: Why must you write `expect(() => f(), throwsStateError)` rather than `expect(f(), throwsStateError)`?
options: The closure makes the test async
Without the closure, f() throws before expect runs, failing the test
It is only a style preference
quiz.explain: expect needs to call the function itself so it can catch and check the exception.

concepts.name: The event loop and microtasks
concepts.summary: Understand Dart's single-threaded event loop, the microtask and event queues, and the exact ordering of async code.
concepts.why: Ordering bugs, frozen UIs and flaky tests come from misunderstanding when async callbacks actually run.
concepts.body:
Each isolate (an independent Dart worker, see the next lesson) runs one thread with an **event loop**, which repeatedly picks the next job to run, and two queues:

- The **microtask queue** — short internal follow-ups: `scheduleMicrotask`, `Future.microtask`, and the follow-up steps of futures that have already finished, including the code after an `await`.
- The **event queue** — external events: timers (`Future.delayed`, `Timer`, `Future(...)`), finished file and network reads, taps and key presses, messages from other isolates, and in Flutter, frame callbacks.

The loop runs the current synchronous code to completion, then **drains the entire microtask queue**, then takes one event, and repeats. So:

- Synchronous code is never interrupted. A long loop on the main isolate freezes the app's screen because no events (including frames) can run.
- Microtasks always run before the next timer, even `Future.delayed(Duration.zero)`.
- Too many microtasks starve the event queue, delaying I/O and frames.

An `async` function runs synchronously up to its first `await`. When the awaited future completes, the rest of the function is scheduled as a microtask. `await` on a non-future value still yields to the microtask queue.

`Future(() => ...)` schedules on the event queue; `Future.value(x).then(...)` and `Future.sync` run the callback in a microtask or immediately. **Zones** (`runZonedGuarded`) are contexts that follow code across `await`s; Flutter uses them to catch async errors nobody else caught.

For heavy CPU work, async doesn't help; move it to another isolate.
takeaways: Sync code runs to completion; then all microtasks; then one event
`await` continuations and `then` on completed futures are microtasks
Timers and `Future()` go on the event queue, after all microtasks
pitfalls: Doing heavy synchronous work in an async function and expecting it not to block the UI.

quiz.q: Which prints first: a `Future.delayed(Duration.zero, ...)` callback or a `scheduleMicrotask` callback scheduled after it?
options: The delayed callback, because it was scheduled first
The microtask, because the microtask queue drains before any event
quiz.explain: The event loop always empties the microtask queue before taking the next event such as a timer.

concepts.name: Isolates and parallelism
concepts.summary: Run CPU-heavy work in parallel with Isolate.run, communicate with ports, and know what can be sent between isolates.
concepts.why: Isolates are Dart's only way to use multiple cores and keep a Flutter UI at 60+ fps during heavy work.
concepts.body:
Dart code runs in **isolates**: each has its own memory and event loop, and isolates **share no mutable state**. That's why Dart needs no locks — and why parallelism requires message passing.

The simplest API is **`Isolate.run`** (Dart 2.19+):

```dart
final result = await Isolate.run(() => parseHugeJson(text));
```

It spawns an isolate, runs the function, returns its result and shuts the isolate down. Flutter's `compute(fn, arg)` is a wrapper around the same idea. Use it for work that takes more than a few milliseconds: JSON decoding of large payloads, image processing, encryption, search indexing.

For long-lived workers, use `Isolate.spawn` with a **`SendPort`/`ReceivePort`** pair: the worker sends back its own `SendPort`, and both sides exchange messages.

What can be sent: most objects are **copied** (deep copy), including lists, maps, records and instances of your classes. Exceptions: objects tied to something outside Dart, such as an open network connection (`Socket`), a `ReceivePort` or a loaded C library (`DynamicLibrary`), can't be sent. Closures can be sent only if what they capture is sendable — capturing a big object by accident copies it too. `Isolate.exit` transfers the result without copying when ending a worker; `TransferableTypedData` moves large blocks of bytes cheaply.

Isolates spawned from the same isolate group share code and start quickly (tens of microseconds to milliseconds). On the web, isolates aren't available in the same form; use web workers.
takeaways: Isolates have separate memory and communicate only by messages
`Isolate.run` (or Flutter's `compute`) offloads one CPU-heavy task
Messages are copied; native resources can't be sent
pitfalls: Capturing a large object in the closure passed to `Isolate.run`, silently copying it to the new isolate.

quiz.q: Why doesn't Dart need mutexes for ordinary objects shared between isolates?
options: Isolates don't share mutable memory; data is copied or transferred in messages
The VM locks every object automatically
Only one isolate runs at a time
quiz.explain: Each isolate has its own heap, so there is no shared mutable state to protect.

concepts.name: Compilation, runtime and the type system
concepts.summary: Know how Dart compiles (JIT, AOT, JS, Wasm), what soundness guarantees at run time, and how tree shaking and the GC affect apps.
concepts.why: Expert decisions about startup time, binary size, web targets and generated code depend on how the toolchain works.
concepts.body:
Dart has several compilation targets:

- **JIT** (`dart run`, Flutter debug builds): the Dart runtime compiles code while the program runs, which enables **hot reload**: new code is swapped into the running program while all its data is kept.
- **AOT** (`dart compile exe`, Flutter release builds): machine code compiled ahead of time with a small runtime, fast startup and no JIT. Reflection (code inspecting classes while running, via `dart:mirrors`) is unavailable, which is why Dart relies on code generation (`build_runner` with generators such as `json_serializable`).
- **Web**: `dart compile js` (dart2js, optimized JavaScript) and `dart compile wasm` (WasmGC, used by Flutter web's `--wasm` builds).

AOT and web builds perform **tree shaking**: unreachable code is removed, so binary size depends on what you actually call.

The type system is **sound**: static types are guaranteed at run time, enforced by the compiler plus a few run-time checks — explicit casts (`as`), covariant generics, and covariant parameters. Soundness lets AOT compilers trust types: they can store numbers directly, call methods without looking them up, and skip null checks.

Memory is managed by a **garbage collector** that frees objects no longer used. It is generational: a fast pass cleans up new objects often (most objects are short-lived), and a slower one, running alongside your code, handles long-lived ones. Creating short-lived objects is cheap, but in Flutter creating large objects on every frame still causes pauses; reuse them in code that runs very often.

`dart:ffi` calls C code directly when compiled to machine code, with `NativeFinalizer` tying C resource lifetimes to Dart objects.
concepts.code:
# Development: JIT with fast edit/run cycles and hot reload in Flutter
dart run bin/main.dart

# Native self-contained executable (AOT, tree-shaken)
dart compile exe bin/main.dart -o build/tool
./build/tool

# Smaller AOT snapshot run by dartaotruntime
dart compile aot-snapshot bin/main.dart

# Web targets
dart compile js -O2 web/main.dart -o build/main.js
dart compile wasm web/main.dart -o build/main.wasm

# Generate code instead of reflection (e.g. json_serializable)
dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
takeaways: JIT enables hot reload; AOT gives fast startup and no reflection
Soundness lets compilers trust static types for optimization
Generational GC makes short-lived objects cheap, but avoid big per-frame allocations
pitfalls: Expecting `dart:mirrors` reflection to work in Flutter or AOT builds — use code generation.

quiz.q: Why do Dart AOT targets rely on code generation (e.g. json_serializable) instead of reflection?
options: Generated code runs only on the web
dart:mirrors isn't available in AOT/Flutter, and generated code allows tree shaking
quiz.explain: Mirrors would defeat tree shaking and aren't supported by the AOT toolchains, so code is generated at build time.
